claims.text: The onset and progression of premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by localized melting at surface-defect sites.
Defect-rich surface regions lower the effective melting barrier.
Nanoparticles with more surface imperfections begin to liquefy below the bulk melting point.
Limited atomic mobility associated with the nanoscale particles constrains completion of melting.
Incomplete melting leads to structural rearrangements such as particle splitting or coalescence.
The starting particles are initially solid, single-phase FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles approximately 5–10 nm in diameter.
The relevant structural mediator is the density and distribution of surface dislocations, vacancies, and edge irregularities.
High local surface energy at defect sites lowers the energy required for atomic rearrangement and initiates localized melting.
Defect-mediated melting produces partial liquid formation and morphology distinct from that of nearly defect-free nanoparticles.
Higher-defect FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will show partial-melting features at a lower temperature than nearly defect-free particles under the same thermal profile.
The defect-induced difference in transition-onset temperature is likely to be on the order of tens of kelvin.
Defect-rich particles will exhibit distinct morphological evolution, including droplets, coalescence, or splitting.
Particles with minimal surface defects remain solid without localized melting until the conventional bulk melting temperature is reached.
The proposed behavior applies to particles in the approximately 5–10 nm size range under rapid or controlled thermal ramps in an inert atmosphere.
The role of surface defects may diminish at larger particle sizes or substantially different heating rates.
Defective carbon edge planes can serve as preferred nucleation and anchoring sites for supported metal nanoparticles and suppress their high-temperature aggregation.
The controlled test compares composition- and size-matched FeNiCrCoCu particles having low versus intentionally enhanced surface-defect densities under identical heating and atmosphere.
The hypothesis is falsified if the low- and high-defect groups show no statistically significant difference in partial-melting onset temperature or morphological evolution.
